title: Granular weight fetch controller and KV cache coordination runbook
content:
Purpose and scope:
This document defines an operational runbook and design notes for a fine-grained Weight Fetch Controller (WFC) that coordinates: lazy loading of model parameters, mmap residency tracking, safetensors unpack fallback, and KV-cache (key-value attention cache) admission/eviction policies. It emphasizes interaction points with the request scheduler, per-request priority, and hot-swap/rollback semantics for model updates.

Goals:
- Provide low-latency warm-path for hot prefixes while minimizing GPU memory footprint for large models.
- Ensure predictable fallbacks (safetensors -> mmap -> remote fetch) with integrity checks and measurable SLOs.
- Maintain KV-cache correctness and avoid thrashing under workload bursts by coordinating admissions with weight residency.
- Define operational safety for hot-swap (model weight activation) with quick rollback and minimal in-flight disruption.

High-level architecture overview:
- Weight Fetch Controller (WFC): per-node controller responsible for deciding when to fetch shard ranges to local GPU memory (or to fall back to remote execution). It exposes an async API used by the request path and by background prefetch workers.
- Residency Map: lightweight bitmap + LRU timestamps per-shard per-GPU. Tracks residency, last-accessed, and pin-count. Persisted ephemeral metadata in /var/lib/redwood/weights/residency for crash recovery.
- Prefetcher threads: background workers that consume hints from the scheduler (upcoming requests, popular prefixes) and from telemetry (token distribution) to warm shards.
- Safetensors Unpacker: local disk unpacking path that can be async or sync depending on urgency; checksum-verified before activation.
- KV-cache admission gate: co-located policy that factors GPU memory pressure, current KV-hit rate, and per-request priority. KV entries are soft-evictable; the gate can be tuned to reduce KV admission when weight residency is low for the requested layers.

Load paths and fallbacks (ordered by preference):
1) Memory resident weight: immediate execution path.
2) Mmap-resident page(s): transient page fault handling path that can service reads via on-demand soft page-in.
3) Safetensors local file not unpacked: request triggers async unpack + atomic install (hot-swap path) or falls back to remote execution if latency budget is tight.
4) Remote weight fetch (RPC to weight-store): used as last resort, expected high latency.

Residency model and shard granularity:
- Shard unit: a contiguous set of tensors that align with the model's logical layers (not raw bytes). Primary reason: per-layer eviction is intuitive for KV coherence and operator kernel alignment. Typical shard sizes: 8MB - 64MB depending on model and hw.
- Residency map tracks: {shard_id -> resident_gpus:list, pin_count:int, last_access_iso_ts}. This is modeled as a flattened structure in the runtime (not nested) for fast lookup.
- Pinning semantics: During active request inference, shards used by the request are pinned (pin_count++) until request completes. Prefetch pins are ephemeral and have a low TTL.

WFC decision logic (simplified):
- On request arrival: compute required shard set S for the request's model/version/seq_len. Ask WFC: are all shards resident on candidate GPU?
  - If yes: proceed.
  - If some shards missing: consult scheduler to decide: (A) re-route to a GPU that has residency, (B) wait for async prefetch with a bounded wait (configurable wait_ms), (C) kick synchronous load/unpack and degrade KV admission for this request, or (D) fallback to remote.
- Synchronous load is allowed only when request's priority >= sync-load-threshold and predicted load latency + remaining budget <= SLO headroom.

Prefetch heuristics and telemetry integration:
- Windowed popularity: maintain sliding window of layer access counts per-model. If a layer exceeds popularity threshold (e.g., top-k by token accesses) prefetch if not resident.
- Prefix-aware prefetch: for chat-like workloads, first N tokens of a prompt produce a predictable layer-access pattern; use cached traces to prefetch top-m shards for high-prob prefixes.
- Burst damping: when a spike is detected, cap prefetch throughput to avoid saturating disk or network. Prefetcher uses leaky-bucket.

KV-cache coordination policies:
- Admission control: when a request would insert KV entries, check memory pressure of both weights and KV. If combined pressure would exceed target utilization (e.g., 85%), then apply one of: 1) deny KV admission; 2) evict lower-priority KV entries; 3) trigger opportunistic weight eviction for cold shards.
- Eviction ranking: composite score = alpha * kv_age + beta * kv_access_freq + gamma * shard_hotness. Tune weights alpha/beta/gamma empirically.
- Consistency: KV entries reference layer shard ids and version stamps. On hot-swap (model version change), invalidate KV entries whose version stamp != active model stamp. This avoids stale attention maps across model variants.

Hot-swap activation protocol (atomic commit):
- Two-phase activation:
  1) Stage: new weights are fetched/unpacked into a quarantine area (on-disk or staging GPU memory). Checksums verified. Compatibility checks (shape/metadata) run.
  2) Commit: switch model routing to new weight set by updating a model-version pointer used by the router and incrementing a global epoch. Each worker receives the epoch bump and atomically maps to new shards.
- In-flight requests: workers that started under old epoch are allowed to complete with old weights. New requests routed to new epoch. This reduces tail effects but raises transient memory pressure during overlap window. The WFC must ensure memory headroom for commit window or perform staggered rollouts by GPU group.
- Rollback: commit record must be durably written. Rollback path unloads new residency (if pinned by commit) and decrements epoch; router switches back. Rollback must be tested end-to-end in pre-prod.

Mmap and safetensors interplay:
- Preferred disk artifact: compressed safetensors (deduplicated, chunked). Primary load step is to unpack the safetensors file into a contiguous mmap-able file (or into an index that allows zero-copy mmapping of chunks).
- Safe unpack strategy: unpack into /var/lib/redwood/weights/unpacking/<model>-<ver>-<part>.tmp -> fsync -> rename to final. Use checksums and file-length guards to avoid partial reads.
- Mmap residency: if file is mmap-able, we rely on OS to page in on demand for cold reads. WFC monitors page-fault rate per-file to decide when to proactively warm pages.

Operator and metrics (what to measure):
- Metrics exposed per model/version and per-node: shard_residency_ratio, prefetch_hit_rate, sync_load_count, async_prefetch_count, page_fault_rate, safetensors_unpack_time, avg_sync_load_latency, kv_admission_rate, kv_eviction_rate, hot_swap_commit_time, rollback_count.
- Alerts: sustained page_fault_rate > X for > Y minutes; sync_load_count spike without prefetch signals broken prefetch heuristics; rollback_count > 0 during a release indicates failure.

APIs and runtime primitives:
- WFC.reserve_shards(request_id, list_of_shard_ids, priority, wait_ms) -> {status: string, missing_shards: list}.
- WFC.pin_shards(request_id, list_of_shard_ids) / WFC.unpin_shards(request_id, list_of_shard_ids).
- WFC.prefetch_hint(model, prefix_signature, priority_hint).
- WFC.query_residency(model, shard_id) -> {resident_gpus: list, last_access_iso_ts: string}.
(These are intentionally flat-return to keep runtime integration fast.)

Operational runbook snippets (quick actions):
- If page_fault_rate high on node X: reduce prefetcher throughput, increase prefetch threshold for popularity; inspect IO queue length and disk latency.
- If hot-swap commit fails with checksum mismatch: mark artifact as corrupted, rollback epoch, trigger artifact re-pull from origin, page operator.
- If KV eviction thrashing: temporarily throttle KV admission to 20% and scale down batch sizes to lower ephemeral memory.

Open questions and tradeoffs:
- Shard sizing: smaller shards reduce wasted memory but increase metadata overhead and more frequent page faults. Need an empirical sweep per-model family.
- Overlap window for hot-swap: full-epoch overlap gives zero-error switching but doubles memory transient; staggered partial rollouts reduce memory but increase complexity.
- Mmap vs explicit io: rely on OS paging for large model streaming simplifies code but gives less control; explicit async IO allows smarter page ordering but requires more engineering.

Experimentation plan (A/B tests):
- Test A: aggressive prefetch (prefetch top-10 popular shards) vs conservative (top-3) on a mixed chat workload. Metrics: tail latency 95/99, disk IO bytes, sync_load_count.
- Test B: KV admission disabled for background-prefetched requests vs enabled. Metrics: quality (LLM eval on held prompts), cost (GPU memory), latency.

Todo and next steps:
- [ ] Implement WFC.reserve_shards API and wire into router (owner: Maya).
- [ ] Add per-shard residency persistence on start-up for quick recovery (owner: Evan).
- [ ] Create integration test that simulates hot-swap with in-flight requests and measures rollback time (owner: Liam).
- [ ] Schedule kernel alignment meeting with runtime-ops to discuss shard layer alignment with fused attention kernels.

Notes to self:
- Keep runbook small and prescriptive; engineers want actionable thresholds.
- Include safe defaults: conservative prefetch, 100ms sync-load wait cap, commit overlap TTL 30s.

Appendix: short pseudocode for request flow:
- request_handler(req):
    shards = model.resolve_shards(req.model, req.seq_len)
    resp = WFC.reserve_shards(req.id, shards, req.priority, wait_ms=100)
    if resp.status == "ok":
        WFC.pin_shards(req.id, shards)
        try:
            exec_with_local_weights(req)
        finally:
            WFC.unpin_shards(req.id, shards)
    else:
        route = scheduler.find_alt_gpu(req, shards)
        if route: forward(req, route)
        else: fallback_to_remote(req)

End of document.
